title: The temple destroyed
hookLine: Abdali blew up the Harmandir; tradition says a flying brick struck his nose

cards: Barrels are carried across the causeway to the Harmandir, the temple in the middle of the pool. Gunpowder. They're packed inside, among the walls where the Granth's hymns had been sung morning and evening.
The Sikh families who might have stood there are dead or scattered after Kup Rahira. Ahmad Shah Abdali has come to Amritsar. The fuse is lit.
Then the blast, and the stones and bricks fly. Tradition adds a detail Sikhs still tell: a brick flew from the explosion and struck Abdali on the nose.

teach.b: Don't hurry past the loss. The Harmandir was the Gurus' house, built in the pool Guru Arjan had finished, where the Granth had been installed. Now it was rubble, and tradition says the pool was filled in again.
For Sikhs who heard the news, it came on top of the dead at Kup Rahira. The building fell. That's the line, and it's meant to be said plainly.

teach.h: A BRICK, AND A WOUND THAT LINGERED.
teach.b: Now the brick. Tradition says the wound on Abdali's nose never properly healed, and some tellings say it troubled him for the rest of his life. That link belongs to the story, not to a record.
Sikhs tell it not as a joke and not quite as a miracle, but as a sign that what's done to the Guru's house doesn't simply go away. So what did Sikhs say was lost, and what wasn't?

teach.h: THE GURU: THE GRANTH AND THE PANTH.
teach.b: Guru Gobind Singh, before his death, had said the Guru from then on would be the Granth, the scripture, and the Panth, the community of the Khalsa. Sikhs say neither could be blown up with a building.
That doesn't make the loss small. People had prayed in that room; their parents had prayed there. But it changes what kind of loss it is.
Guru Tegh Bahadur has a line in the Granth, in paraphrase: whatever has been made will pass away, today or tomorrow. The Sikh scripture doesn't promise that buildings last. It points past them.
So today, just sit with what fell. What comes next is tomorrow's story.

how: Sikhs remember the destruction of the Harmandir by Ahmad Shah Abdali as part of the eighteenth-century persecutions, and teach that the Guru is the Guru Granth Sahib and the Guru Panth, not any building.

games.q: you're a Sikh who has just heard the Harmandir has been blown up, so soon after Kup Rahira. what do you do first?
o: tell yourself it was only a building and move on.
let it be a real loss, and grieve it.

games.why: the story keeps the loss real: the building fell. what the Sikhs did next is tomorrow's story, at the ruins.

practice: Bring to mind a place that's gone, a childhood home, a shop that closed, a room where someone you loved used to sit, and see it as it was, without rushing to the bright side.
Then notice, gently, what you still carry from it that no one could knock down, and if you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Harimandar, the house of God. Ahmad Shah Abdali had it blown up with gunpowder, and tradition says a flying brick struck him on the nose; the building fell, but Sikhs say the Guru did not. Today's word.
